screenings.title: Center Stage
screenings.description: Hong Kong, 1991 Directed by Stanley Kwan Starring Maggie Cheung, Han Chin, Carina Lau, Tony Leung Ka-fai In Cantonese, Mandarin, and English Approx. 155 min. International superstar Maggie Cheung (IN THE MOOD FOR LOVE) embodies tragic screen siren Ruan Lingyu, known as the “Greta Garbo of China,” in this unconventional biopic by Hong Kong New Wave master Stanley Kwan (ROUGE). Praised for her moving and emotive onscreen presence, Ruan’s private life, which was frequent fodder for the vicious Shanghai tabloids, began to mirror the melodramas which brought her fame, culminating in her suicide at age 24. Kwan and Cheung paint a kaleidoscopic yet intimate portrait of the ill-fated actress, deftly blending lush period drama, archival footage, and metatextual documentary sequences of Cheung reflecting on Ruan’s legacy. The result is, much like the films of Ruan Lingyu themselves, “tender, vivid, and almost overwhelmingly moving” (Time Out). Presented by Fortune Star Media Limited, the restoration of the film was carried out from the original 35mm picture and optical soundtrack negative. The prints were repaired, cleaned and scanned in Hong Kong, then digitally restored in 4K resolution in Bologna, Italy by L'Immagine Ritrovata. Endorsed by the director, Stanley Kwan, the color correction was completed by Interface Video Production Ltd in Hong Kong. Presented with support from The Reginald S. Reinhardt, Ling-Makekau Fund for Asia-Pacific Films A FILM MOVEMENT RELEASE

screenings.title: Otar Iosseliani Early Shorts Program
screenings.description: A program of the inspired early shorts that established Iosseliani at the forefront of a new, rising generation of Georgian filmmakers. Featuring Akvarel, in which a quarreling working-class couple experience a revelation at an art exhibition; Sapovnela, in which an old man who tends exquisite flower gardens in the hills around Mtskheta sees his life’s work threatened by the arrival of a new road; April, in which a young couple find their happiness dwindling as their comfort increases upon moving into a brand new, squeaky clean housing development, and Tudzhi (Cast Iron), a documentary description of life in an ironworks that singles out individuals on the factory floor not as symbols of thrumming Soviet industrial might, but as human beings.

screenings.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day
screenings.description: Four years have passed since the events of No Way Home, and Peter is now an adult living entirely alone, having voluntarily erased himself from the lives and memories of those he loves. Crime-fighting in a New York that no longer knows his name, he’s devoted himself entirely to protecting his city — a full-time Spider-Man — but as the demands on him intensify, the pressure sparks a surprising physical evolution that threatens his existence, even as a strange new pattern of crimes gives rise to one of the most powerful threats he has ever faced.

screenings.title: Late Fame
screenings.description: Willem Dafoe is Ed Saxberger, a postal worker whose former life as a downtown poet in late-70s New York is rediscovered by a young admirer (Donovan) and his “Enthusiasm Society,” a group of 20-somethings with a comically romanticized sense of the past. In the company of his new friends, including the mysterious and mercurial Gloria (Lee of PAST LIVES), Ed has the uncanny feeling of merging with his younger self. Directed by Kent Jones (DIANE) from a witty, razor-sharp script by Samy Burch (MAY DECEMBER), LATE FAME is a funny, lively, poignant, and occasionally haunting New York story. Presented with support from The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film 2025 96 MIN. USA MAGNOLIA PICTURES

screenings.title: Wild Inside
screenings.description: Also playing: the 14-minute documentary short DREAM OF BIRDS screens with the 11:00am shows of WILD INSIDE Friday, July 31-Thursday August 6 only. Following a unique study led by Argentine physicist Gabriel Mindlin, DREAM OF BIRDS playfully explores the mystery of music through the mathematical patterns behind birdsong, and how our lives and relationships are rhythmically organized.

screenings.title: White Nights
screenings.description: Italy, 1957 Directed by Luchino Visconti Based on the short story by Fyodor Dostoevsky Starring Marcello Mastroianni, Maria Schell, Jean Marais Music by Nino Rota In Italian with English subtitles Approx 103 min. “Visconti’s version of the Dostoevsky story—about the chance encounter of a couple as she is waiting in vain for her lover, and the obsessive, panic-stricken relationship which then develops between them—later filmed by Bresson as FOUR NIGHTS OF A DREAMER. Visconti traps his characters (three excellent performances) within a claustrophobic canal-side set, and the film is a series of brief walks, chases, attempted escapes, always frustrated. Shot as neo-realist high tragedy, the film offers its characters only one strange moment of escape from their night-time obsessions—a raucous, sexual, subversive scene in a dance-hall. Then the snow comes down, and with it a chilly desperation about the extent of human self-delusion.” – Time Out Restored by Luce Cinecittà, from the original 35mm negative Presented with support from the Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film A JANUS FILMS RELEASE

screenings.title: A Sad and Beautiful World
screenings.description: In this sweeping love story that spans three decades of passion, heartbreak and hope, Nino and Yasmina find themselves drawn together by a magnetic relationship. As they face an impossible choice between love and survival, they must decide if they want to build a family and chart a path to happiness in Lebanon, despite the tragedies ravaging the country. In Arabic with English subtitles.

screenings.title: The Flying Dutchman
screenings.description: “DEFA’s The Flying Dutchman is considered the first attempt to film a Wagner opera in its entirety, although, in point of fact, it too reworks the story to suit both the cinematic medium and the political viewpoint of the GDR. It was directed by opera director Joachim Herz, who, perhaps because it was his first (and only) film, opted to experiment with state-of-the-art sound and film techniques. Director Herz dramatically changes Wagner’s opera from one about a ghostly event to the reveries of a young woman named Senta who is infatuated with the story of the Flying Dutchman. To separate reality from Senta’s imagination, Mr. Herz uses two different film aspect ratios. Whenever we are watching Anna in the real world, the aspect ratio is [in 1.67:1]. When the film shifts to Senta’s dream world, the screen slowly opens up to the 2.35:1 dimensions of DEFA’s Totalvision (the same as Cinemascope). In other films that use multiple aspect ratios, the change in screen aspect is handled as edits, but Herz wanted these switches in perspective to flow like the film’s lush score. To do this required sophisticated in-camera techniques involving animation frames and an American Mitchell camera that accepted double reels. This process meant that everything had to be shot with the larger format while the animation frame was simultaneously running through the camera. That this worked at all is a testament to cinematographer Erich Gusko’s skill with a camera.” – Jim Morton

screenings.title: Jimmy
screenings.description: Shot in dreamy 16mm black and white, Yasshadai Owens’ debut feature Jimmy offers an intimate, speculative portrait of what a young James Baldwin may have experienced during his first trip to Paris in 1948. (credit: Toronto International Film Festival)

screenings.title: First Blood
screenings.description: The movie whose runaway success singlehandedly landed Carolco in the ranks of legit Tinseltown players, Kotcheff’s taut adaptation of David Morrell’s 1972 novel of the same name introduces Sylvester Stallone as burnt-out Vietnam vet John Rambo, in the words of critic J. Hoberman, a combination of “super-grunt, Green Beret, hippie protester, VC guerilla, righteous outlaw [and] Hollywood Freedom Fighter.” Arriving in the town of Hope, Washington State, after paying his respects to an old army buddy who’s died from the lingering effects of Agent Orange exposure, Rambo is escorted to the city limits by hard-ass local sheriff Brian Dennehy who, with this slight, unwittingly lights the fuse on a human stick of dynamite. As Colonel Trautman (Richard Crenna), Rambo’s old superior officer, says upon arriving in Hope to prevent a slaughter: “I didn’t come to save Rambo from you. I came to save you from Rambo.”

screenings.title: The Night is Short, Walk on Girl
screenings.description: A surreal nocturnal animated odyssey from Yuasa, the mad genius behind Mind Game, rendered in a frenetic, galaxy-brained, endlessly morphing style. The Night is Short, Walk on Girl follows a mysterious high schooler known only as The Girl with Black Hair through the streets of Kyoto’s famed Ponto-Cho party district, drinking middle-aged salarymen under the table when she’s not mixing with barflies, obsessive collectors, and guerilla theater performers, all the while oblivious to the efforts of a fellow student who has been creating increasingly fantastic and contrived reasons to run into her in a gambit to win her love. A comic fable of fleeting youthful passions, as lived out through one mad, unforgettable night.

screenings.title: Julian
screenings.description: Fleur and Julian fall madly in love and decide to get married in all countries where they, as two women, are allowed to do so. But after only four marriages, their journey comes to a painful and unexpected halt.

screenings.title: The Invite
screenings.description: Joe (Seth Rogen) and Angela’s (Olivia Wilde) marriage is on thin ice. When they invite their enigmatic upstairs neighbors (Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton) for a dinner party, the night spirals into unexpected places. Have they reignited the spark or lit the match that burns it all down? A remake of the 2020 Spanish film The People Upstairs, Olivia Wilde’s star-studded take on a dinner party dramedy (written by Will McCormack and Rashida Jones) is a timely portrait of a modern marriage, teeming with wit, belly laughs, and a surprising poignancy.

screenings.title: Riverdogs
screenings.description: U.S., 1978 Directed by Robb Moss Approx. 32 min. In 1978, Robb Moss was 28 years old, a former river guide in the Mountain West and dreaming of a career as a filmmaker. One fall, on a month-long Grand Canyon rafting adventure with a group of friends, he collected the footage that would form the basis for his first film, the now-celebrated Riverdogs, a glorious sun-drenched ode to youth and nature, to life lived, often without clothing, at the brink of the possible. Shot on 16mm, scenes of communal play and risky outdoor adventuring are stacked one upon another creating a portrait of joy, vigor, and freedom. At the end of the trip, the group convened a vote: should they all stay together or head home? While they didn’t know it, they were on the verge of no longer being young.

screenings.title: Commodity Trading: Dies Irae (w/q&a)
screenings.description: A prologue, epilogue, and appendix all at once for COMMODITY TRADING: DIES IRAE, M. Woods returns with a doctor’s bag of disassociative-media booster shots. Direct animation, inter-media collage, appropriation, vitriolic poetry, cursed family travelogues, and music videos make up this hellish cocktail. Including works preceding and following the creation of Woods’ feature and riding along interrelated streams of consciousness, titles screened in this showcase have rarely (if ever) seen a NY audience –including a few cathartic rows against Spectacle’s reluctant home of modern day Williamsburg, Brooklyn.

A harsh but cautiously hopeful depiction of the lives of young Afro-French women, and the unique adversities they face.

screenings.title: Dumplings
screenings.description: Expanding his segment of the same name in the horror anthology film Three… Extremes, Chan’s Dumplings tells the deliciously deviant tale of ex-soap star Mrs. Li (Miriam Yeung) who, her looks fading and husband Tony Leung Ka-fai’s eye wandering, begins supplementing her diet with a special preparation of the eponymous foodstuff that uses the flesh of unborn fetuses for filling. Christopher Doyle’s photography, along with the work of production designer Yee Chung-man, provide an elegant setting to this baleful, bleak fable described by its director as a “post-feminist horror movie,” a work that may or may not have exercised its influence on a little picture called The Substance.

When he makes a series of high-stakes bets that could lead to the windfall of a lifetime, Howard must perform a precarious high-wire act, balancing business, family, and encroaching adversaries on all sides, in his relentless pursuit of the ultimate win.

screenings.title: The Fence
screenings.description: A vast public works project in West Africa. Horn (Matt Dillon), the construction site manager, and Cal (Tom Blyth), a young engineer, share lodging behind the double gates of their compound. Leone (Mia McKenna-Bruce), Horn’s recent bride, comes to join them the same night that a man (Isaach De Bankole) appears at the fence. His name is Alboury. Like a specter in the darkness, he demands the body of his brother who died earlier that day on the site. He will hound the two men all night long until they return it, as Leone watches the disaster play out before her.

screenings.title: Wild Inside
screenings.description: Also playing: the 14-minute documentary short DREAM OF BIRDS screens with the 11:00am shows of WILD INSIDE Friday, July 31-Thursday August 6 only. Following a unique study led by Argentine physicist Gabriel Mindlin, DREAM OF BIRDS playfully explores the mystery of music through the mathematical patterns behind birdsong, and how our lives and relationships are rhythmically organized.

screenings.title: Olmo
screenings.description: Olmo just wants to be a normal teenager and hang out with his best friend, but he must help care for his bedridden father. When Olmo gets invited to a party by his beautiful neighbor, he will do whatever he can to meet up with her while embarking on an adventure of mischief, laughs, and chaos. As the night unfolds, he may come to love the very place he’s spent so long trying to escape: his home. In English and Spanish with English subtitles.

screenings.title: Dread Beat an Blood
screenings.description: About DREAD BEAT AN BLOOD: “[A] gem... a portrait of the artist as principled activist.” – Sasha Frere-Jones, 4Columns “Fantastic... An amazing snapshot of the time of the pre-Brixton riots... This is so relevant a movie. That’s what makes it so good.” – Gilles Peterson, BBC “A fascinating document of LKJ in his time and place, touring with the sound systems, strolling through the market and visiting Tulse Hill schools, vividly capturing black British culture in a country on the cusp of Thatcherism, just a few months before the Brixton uprising.” – Stephen Troussé, Uncut “An invaluable document of Brixton, an area that was already at the front lines of the anti-racist struggle, the streets in which people would soon rise up in rebellion. That sense of latent frustration simmers in every frame. It is Johnson himself who articulates that frustration, honing that anger into art via his poetry.” – Kevin Mccaighy, The Quietus About Linton Kwesi Johnson: “If any young artists need to know about longevity and integrity, Linton Kwesi Johnson is the one to look to... He knew his path and he walked it. His words are still relevant and that reggae bass is still vibrating.” – Steve McQueen “Linton Kwesi Johnson’s impact on the cultural landscape over the last half-century has been colossal and multi-generational.” – The Guardian “He’s written the anthems for a generation who felt oppressed and victimized... He’s now celebrated as one of this country’s most influential cultural commentators.” – BBC “A revolutionary poet for our times.” – Jacobin “The Poet Laureate of Black Britain.” – Paul Gilroy “The roots of hip-hop run deep, and among the deepest branches remains Linton Kwesi Johnson, the Jamaican-born, British-raised poet, writer, and performer often hailed as the father of dub poetry.” – David Browne, Rolling Stone

screenings.title: Michael Mann's Manhunter: The Final Cut
screenings.description: Mann’s genre-defining serial-killer thriller returns in a stunning new restoration overseen by the filmmaker himself. A retired criminal profiler (William Petersen) reluctantly returns to the FBI to help track down a murderer and is forced to consult an expert—the imprisoned Dr. Hannibal Lecktor (Brian Cox in a subtly chilling performance). Adapted from the first of Thomas Harris’s Lecktor novels, MANHUNTER’s supporting cast includes Tom Noonan as the hunted killer, and three-time Oscar nominee Joan Allen.

screenings.title: Roller Junkies
screenings.description: Hollywood-sleaze auteur Jared Masters is an LA based, low budget filmmaker, creating an array of women-centric features inspired by VHS slashers and 60’s B-movies. His films represent a modern take on genre films, and have John Waters/Kuchar Brothers humor to them. Jared refers to himself as a modern cult filmmaker, occasionally starring in the films he makes. The three films selected are an introduction to his filmography, highlighting his taste for camp and self-aware humor, backed by a clear love for cinema. Masters works align with the Spectacle vision to highlight underrated, seldom-viewed filmmakers and late-night summer indies.

screenings.title: Millennium Mambo
screenings.description: A stylish and seductive submersion into the techno-scored neon nightlife of Taipei, Hou’s much-misunderstood marvel stars Shu Qi (The Assassin) as an aimless bar hostess drifting away from her blowhard boyfriend and towards Jack Kao’s suave, sensitive gangster. Structured as a flashback to the then-present from the then-future of 2011, it’s a transfixing trance-out of a movie, drenched in club lights, ecstatic endorphin-rush exhilaration, and a nagging undercurrent of ennui. Hou and longtime cinematographer Lee here break from their familiar pattern of elegantly composed long shot long takes to create something both more intimate and hectic, a film whose shallow-focus images, jittery camerawork, and cramped locations evoke both the claustrophobic character of Taiwan’s capital city and, in Lee’s words, “the feeling of youth.”

screenings.title: In the Mood for Love
screenings.description: Wong’s arthouse smash is the very simple tale of two people in early ’60s Hong Kong, Mr. Chow (Tony Leung Chiu-wai) and Mrs. Chen (Maggie Cheung), drawn to one another by the discovery that their spouses are getting together on the side. A little story, full of little details, all surrounding a love affair that isn’t really a love affair—but throbbing with huge, aching emotions that it can barely contain. It might just break your heart.

screenings.title: ∞ Infinity Day: Short Films about Math
screenings.description: This selection of films showing the artists’ take on explorations of math range from simple counting through mind-boggling explanations of the vast and infinitesimal. Program runs 41 minutes. Pinball Number Count #8 Forest Follies Dir. Jeff Hale. 1977, 1 min. U.S. A mainstay of Sesame Street, this iconic animation series of the inside of a pinball machine features a super funky soundtrack and vocals from the Pointer Sisters. Number 8 in the series features unicycling bears and other forest animals. Sesame Street excerpts provided courtesy of Sesame Workshop. Numerosity Number 8 Dir. Jim Henson. 1969, 2 mins, U.S.. The 8th in the ‘”Baker numbers” series for Sesame Street features adults, puppies, and children counting to eight and culminates in the dramatic appearance of a clumsy baker. Courtesy of The Jim Henson Legacy. © Sesame Workshop The Dot and the Line: A Romance in Lower Mathematics Dir. Chuck Jones, co-dir. Maurice Noble. 1965, 10 mins. U.S. A straight blue line is hopelessly in love with a red dot. Based on a book by Norton Juster, author of The Phantom Tollbooth, the film is a more esoteric work from the legendary animation director Chuck Jones, one of the creators of Bugs Bunny and Wile E. Coyote for Looney Tunes. Symmetry Dirs. Charles and Ray Eames. 1961, 3 mins. U.S. One of five “Peep Shows” the iconic designers Charles and Ray Eames created for their IBM-sponsored exhibition, Mathematica, the film introduces the concept of various degrees of symmetry, giving viewers a “peep” of the mathematical concept. © 2026 Eames Office, LLC. All rights reserved. The King of 8 Dir. Jim Henson. 1970, 1 min. U.S. Masterfully created in stop-motion animation by Henson and Don Sahlin, the King of the Land of 8 tells about all the items that number 8 in a rhythmic song. Find the puppets from the film, created by Sahlin, on view in The Jim Henson Exhibition. Courtesy of The Jim Henson Legacy © Sesame Workshop Spheres Dirs. Norman McLaren and René Jodoin. 1969, 8 mins. Canada. In this three-part experiment in geometric abstraction, spheres with metallic reflections float and are propelled through space. Lustrously hand-painted stop-motion animation set to Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier, played by pianist Glenn Gould. Courtesy ONF/NFB Animation vs. Geometry Dir. Alan Becker. 2024, 9 mins. U.S. A yellow stick figure fights its way through an increasingly complex world of vicious angles and polygons. Powers of Ten and the Relative Size of Things in the Universe Dirs. Charles and Ray Eames. 1977, 9 mins. U.S. Investigating the idea of an exponential series, the film illustrates scale and the significance of adding a zero to a number. It begins with a couple picnicking in a park bordering Lake Michigan in Chicago. The journey steadily moves away from the couple, reaching the edge of the known universe, before reversing back down to the atomic level of the hand of the man napping on the picnic blanket. Original music score by Elmer Bernstein. © 2026 Eames Office, LLC. All rights reserved. RSVP recommended. Seating is first come, first served. Open Worlds: Science is funded by Simons Foundation International and administered by the Simons Foundation’s Science, Society & Culture division.

screenings.title: Blades of Glory
screenings.description: Two figure skating rivals are banned from the sport after a brawl over the gold medal. Joining forces, they find a loophole in the rules that allows them to skate again… as a pair!

screenings.title: Thief
screenings.description: Becoming closer to his dream of leading a normal life, a professional safecracker agrees to do a job for the mafia, who have other plans for him. Released in the US as Violent Streets, Michael Mann’s super influential minimalist neo-noir looks as authentic and original today as the day it did in 1981. Mann used real thieves as technical advisors on the film and that Tangerine Dream soundtrack is a joy. Donald Thorin’s moody and brilliant cinematography seals the deal.

screenings.title: Addams Family Values
screenings.description: Sat Aug 8: The Big Cheese Q&A w/dir. Sara Joe Wolansky & subject Adam Moskowitz, moderated by Josh Windsor, after the 7:35 sho

screenings.title: Gummo
screenings.description: Teen friends Tummler (Nick Sutton) and Solomon (Jacob Reynolds) navigate the ruins of a tiny, tornado-ravaged town in Ohio that is populated by the deformed, disturbed and perverted. When not gunning down stray cats for a few bucks, the boys pass their time getting stoned on household inhalants. Elsewhere, the mute Bunny Boy (Jacob Sewell) dons rabbit ears and is bullied by kids half his age, and sisters Dot (Chloe Sevigny) and Helen (Carisa Glucksman) dodge a pedophile.

screenings.title: Satan's Menagerie
screenings.description: Dr. Craymoor (co-writer Thomas V. Powers, doing his best hammy public-access-Vincent Price) is a paranormal talk show host who dabbles in the dark arts in pursuit of fame and riches. We’ll refrain from spoiling the (surprisingly convoluted) plot, but it involves, among other things, a Vietnam vet turned werewolf, a half-man half-amphibian who escapes from a carnival sideshow, and the disciples of a centuries old blood cult called the ‘Sons of Jeramin’.

screenings.title: Ghost in the Shell
screenings.description: “We follow Kusanagi on her hunt for The Puppet Master, a hacker who can access the ‘ghosts’, or souls, of ordinary citizens and carry out cyber-crimes by proxy. Now entirely synthetic, her original human body replaced and improved on piece by piece, Kusanagi is unsure whether her ghost still lingers in her man-made form: in the opening credits, her cybernetic form is assembled in a factory, and the haunting temple chant on the soundtrack makes the process look like a religious rite.

screenings.title: Jimmy
screenings.description: Shot in dreamy 16mm black and white, Yasshadai Owens’ debut feature Jimmy offers an intimate, speculative portrait of what a young James Baldwin may have experienced during his first trip to Paris in 1948. (credit: Toronto International Film Festival)

screenings.title: The Big Cheese
screenings.description: A scrappy team of eccentric American cheesemongers defies tradition to take on the world’s top cheese masters at the Mondial du Fromage, battling cultural clashes, personal struggles, and melting cheese in pursuit of respect, redemption, and a historic victory.

screenings.title: A Child of My Own
screenings.description: This new hybrid documentary from the Oscar-nominated director of The Mole Agent and The Eternal Memory follows the shocking tale of a woman desperate for a baby. Burdened by family and societal expectations, she fakes a pregnancy and gets tangled up in a crime.

screenings.title: Vertigo
screenings.description: Dress up becomes a matter of fevered fixation in Hitchcock’s utterly intoxicating thriller, in which ex-cop-cum-snoop-for-hire Scottie Ferguson (Jimmy Stewart) sets out on a routine job tailing the mysterious Madeline (Kim Novak), an old pal’s wife—and soon finds himself in the center of a whirlpool of romantic obsession and supernatural quandaries, speeding towards a tragic denouement. Perennially on the short list of the greatest films of all time, Hitchcock’s film of death, desire, and doppelgangers—a key inspiration haunting every frame of Chantal Akerman's La Captive—has lost none of its ability to simultaneously seduce and repel. “One of the landmarks—not merely of the movies, but of 20th-century art.”—Dave Kehr, Chicago Reader

screenings.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day
screenings.description: Four years have passed since the events of No Way Home, and Peter is now an adult living entirely alone, having voluntarily erased himself from the lives and memories of those he loves. Crime-fighting in a New York that no longer knows his name, he’s devoted himself entirely to protecting his city — a full-time Spider-Man — but as the demands on him intensify, the pressure sparks a surprising physical evolution that threatens his existence, even as a strange new pattern of crimes gives rise to one of the most powerful threats he has ever faced.

screenings.title: Girlhood
screenings.description: Set in the suburbs of Paris, Sciamma’s coming-of-age story stars Karidja Touré as Marieme, a 16-year-old who finds a sense of sorority, camaraderie, and mutual support when she joins up with an amateur “gang” of girls her age—much to the chagrin of her overbearing, abusive brother. A harsh but cautiously hopeful depiction of the lives of young Afro-French women, and the unique adversities they face.

screenings.title: The Third Man
screenings.description: U.K./U.S., 1949 Directed by Carol Reed Screenplay by Graham Greene Starring Joseph Cotten, Alida Valli, Trevor Howard, and Orson Welles as Harry Lime Music by Anton Karas Cinematography by Robert Krasker WINNER Academy Award® – Best Cinematography, 1950 WINNER Cannes Film Festival – Palme d’Or, 1949 Approx. 104 min. 35mm. In rubble-strewn postwar Vienna, its occupation divided among four powers, Joseph Cotten’s pulp Western writer Holly Martins arrives to meet up with his old friend Harry Lime, only to find that he’s dead—or is he? And as the supremely naïve Cotten, a monoglot stranger in a strange land, descends through the levels of deception, and as he discovers his own friend’s corruption, the moral choices loom. A triumph of atmosphere—with its Vienna locations (including the gigantic Riesenrad ferris wheel and the dripping sewers), its tilted camera angles, its Robert Krasker-shot shadows, and Anton Karas’ unforgettable zither theme—and with its stars in perhaps their most iconic roles: bereted Trevor Howard at his most Britishly military; Alida Valli, here truly enigmatic and Garboesque; and Welles’ Harry Lime, arriving in one of the greatest star entrances ever, and adding the famous “cuckoo clock” speech to Greene’s original script, with the whole topped by its legendary, almost endlessly drawn-out finale shot. Winner of the Palme d’Or at the Cannes Film Festival and an Academy Award® for Best Cinematography, along with many other awards and nominations, THE THIRD MAN has appeared repeatedly on “Best of All-Time” lists of the past 75 years. Presented with support from The Robert Jolin Osborne Endowed Fund for American Classic Cinema of the 1930s, ’40s, and ’50s and The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film A RIALTO PICTURES RELEASE

screenings.title: The Samurai and the Prisoner
screenings.description: When Lord Murashige Araki (Masahiro Motoki) rises up against the tyrannical Nobunaga Oda (Masaki Suda), he finds himself besieged within the walls of his own castle. Isolated, he is confronted with a series of mysterious crimes that shatter the fragile order of his court, plunging the fortress into fear and suspicion. With Oda’s army closing in and a traitor hiding among his ranks, Murashige is forced into an uneasy alliance with Kanbei Kuroda (Masaki Suda), a brilliant yet dangerous strategist held prisoner in the dungeon. Helped by his wife Chiyoho (Yuriko Yoshitaka) and his most loyal generals, Murashige must uncover the truth before the castle falls.

screenings.title: White Nights
screenings.description: Italy, 1957 Directed by Luchino Visconti Based on the short story by Fyodor Dostoevsky Starring Marcello Mastroianni, Maria Schell, Jean Marais Music by Nino Rota In Italian with English subtitles Approx 103 min. “Visconti’s version of the Dostoevsky story—about the chance encounter of a couple as she is waiting in vain for her lover, and the obsessive, panic-stricken relationship which then develops between them—later filmed by Bresson as FOUR NIGHTS OF A DREAMER. Visconti traps his characters (three excellent performances) within a claustrophobic canal-side set, and the film is a series of brief walks, chases, attempted escapes, always frustrated. Shot as neo-realist high tragedy, the film offers its characters only one strange moment of escape from their night-time obsessions—a raucous, sexual, subversive scene in a dance-hall. Then the snow comes down, and with it a chilly desperation about the extent of human self-delusion.” – Time Out Restored by Luce Cinecittà, from the original 35mm negative Presented with support from the Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film A JANUS FILMS RELEASE

screenings.title: Henson Fan Appreciation Day: A Salute to Henson Fans (But Mostly ToughPigs)
screenings.description: If a frog sings in a swamp and no one’s around to hear him, does his banjo make a sound? Where would the Muppets be without their fans? Throughout Henson history, through movies and television shows and reboots and all those quiet moments in between, the fans have kept the spirit of Jim Henson alive. This August, Museum of the Moving Image will be paying tribute to those dedicated fans in the Muppet Theatre audience. That’s you!! To pay homage to the Henson fan community, Jim Henson Legacy President Craig Shemin will be in conversation with members of Muppet fan site ToughPigs.com (celebrating its 25th anniversary) and the admins of the Muppet Wiki. And as a “thank you” to all the dedicated fans, the event will feature a screening of a rare classic production from the Henson vaults! This event is for casual Henson fans, die-hard fanatics, and everyone in between! Whether you have fond memories of watching The Muppet Movie or if you’ve memorized every line of dialogue, MoMI salutes you! Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth (ages 3–17) / free for MoMI members at the Senior/Student level and above. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: A Sad and Beautiful World
screenings.description: In this sweeping love story that spans three decades of passion, heartbreak and hope, Nino and Yasmina find themselves drawn together by a magnetic relationship. As they face an impossible choice between love and survival, they must decide if they want to build a family and chart a path to happiness in Lebanon, despite the tragedies ravaging the country. In Arabic with English subtitles.

screenings.title: Remake
screenings.description: “McElwee is a practitioner of cinema at its most elemental. He’s a man with a movie camera, pointing it at whatever or whoever is around him—which for many years included Adrian—and finding wellsprings of humor, truth, surprise... REMAKE shows him still to be a formidable artist in the face of tragedy, and one whose comically askew sensibility remains intact.” – Zachary Barnes, The Wall Street Journal “Extraordinarily clear-eyed for a work so broken-hearted: at once a home movie, an intimate diary, and an expansive study of the filmmaker’s purpose, constantly disrupting its own conclusions with expressions of anger, amusement, and still-unresolved confusion.” – Guy Lodge, Variety “Incorporation of his late son’s own footage elevates this beautiful, tragic movie from powerful to profound... Each of Ross McElwee’s deeply personal documentaries is built directly atop a fault line that separates—or connects—the microcosmic and the universal. But few films could be more unsparingly intimate than REMAKE.” – Elizabeth Weitzman, The Wrap “Emotionally piercing... meaningful and poignant.” –Warren Cantrell, The Playlist “A complex, layered contemplation of grief, memory, family ties and the meaning of filmmaking as a profoundly personal activity, REMAKE is a richly rewarding experience—emotionally, narratively and philosophically.” – Jonathan Romney, Screen International

screenings.title: American Pachuco
screenings.description: Groundbreaking Chicano activist/director Luis Valdez mounted agitprop performances on flatbed trucks in the 1960s with his El Teatro Campesino, mobilizing California farmworkers to secure their first union contract; authored Zoot Suit, the first Chicano play on Broadway, and directed the 1981 screen adaptation, starring Edward James Olmos; and wrote and directed the highest-grossing Hollywood Latino movie in history, the Ritchie Valens biopic, LA BAMBA. AMERICAN PACHUCO (Valdez defines pachucos as Mexican-American “street cats with style”) playfully tracks his extraordinary life and career, with rarely seen footage from his subversive theater and television work, and interviews with Valdez; actors Olmos (who narrates the film in his ZOOT SUIT pachuco voice), Lou Diamond Phillips, and Cheech Marin; labor activist Dolores Huerta; and Linda Ronstadt. Presented with support from The Robert E. Appel Fund for Spanish and Portuguese Language Films, The Richard Brick, Geri Ashur, and Sara Bershtel Fund for Social Justice Documentaries, and The Roy Lichtenstein Foundation Fund 2026 93 MIN. USA IN ENGLISH AND SPANISH WITH ENGLISH SUBTITLES

screenings.title: Le amiche
screenings.description: Perhaps the first of Antonioni’s films to give a clear indication of the direction of his mature style, this adaptation of Cesare Pavese’s Among Women Only finds glamorous Eleonora Rossi Drago returning to her hometown of Turin to open a branch of a fashion boutique, in the process taking up with the miserable, sniping local smart set and beginning an affair with architect’s assistant Franco Fabrizi. The air of bourgeois discontentment is thick, while the disquieting train station finale is the first of Antonioni’s great set pieces.

screenings.title: Julian

Tsai's beloved film returns to Metrograph for a weeklong run on a newly struck 35mm print, approved by Tsai himself.

screenings.description: Tuesday, June 16 at 7:00: Sneak Preview + Q&A with John Early Wednesday, June 17 at 7:00: Sneak Preview + Q&A with John Early and Carla Lalli Friday, June 19 at 2:15: Q&A with John Early moderated by John Wilson Friday, June 19 at 4:45: Q&A with John Early moderated by Brace Belden Friday, June 19 at 7:15: Q&A with John Early moderated by Ivy Wolk Friday, June 10 at 9:45: Extended introduction by John Early Saturday, June 20 at 11:30: Q&A with John Early moderated by Julio Torres Saturday, June 20 at 2:15: Q&A with John Early moderated by Theda Hammel Saturday, June 20 at 4:45: Q&A with John Early moderated by Sarah Sherman Saturday, June 20 at 7:15: Q&A with John Early moderated by Amy Sedaris Saturday, June 20 at 9:45: Extended introduction by John Early

screenings.title: The Piano - New 4K Restoration
screenings.description: Ada – mute since birth – her nine year old daughter and her piano arrive to an arranged marriage in the remote bush of nineteenth century New Zealand. Of all her belongings her husband refuses to transport the piano and it is left behind on the beach. Unable to bear its certain destruction, Ada strikes a bargain with an illiterate tattooed neighbour. She may earn her piano back if she allows him to do certain things while she plays ; one black key for every lesson. The arrangement draws all three deeper and deeper into a complex emotional, sexual bond remarkable for its naive passion and frightening disregard for limits.

screenings.title: A Sad and Beautiful World
screenings.description: In this sweeping love story that spans three decades of passion, heartbreak and hope, Nino and Yasmina find themselves drawn together by a magnetic relationship. As they face an impossible choice between love and survival, they must decide if they want to build a family and chart a path to happiness in Lebanon, despite the tragedies ravaging the country. In Arabic with English subtitles.

screenings.title: Remake
screenings.description: “McElwee is a practitioner of cinema at its most elemental. He’s a man with a movie camera, pointing it at whatever or whoever is around him—which for many years included Adrian—and finding wellsprings of humor, truth, surprise... REMAKE shows him still to be a formidable artist in the face of tragedy, and one whose comically askew sensibility remains intact.” – Zachary Barnes, The Wall Street Journal “Extraordinarily clear-eyed for a work so broken-hearted: at once a home movie, an intimate diary, and an expansive study of the filmmaker’s purpose, constantly disrupting its own conclusions with expressions of anger, amusement, and still-unresolved confusion.” – Guy Lodge, Variety “Incorporation of his late son’s own footage elevates this beautiful, tragic movie from powerful to profound... Each of Ross McElwee’s deeply personal documentaries is built directly atop a fault line that separates—or connects—the microcosmic and the universal. But few films could be more unsparingly intimate than REMAKE.” – Elizabeth Weitzman, The Wrap “Emotionally piercing... meaningful and poignant.” –Warren Cantrell, The Playlist “A complex, layered contemplation of grief, memory, family ties and the meaning of filmmaking as a profoundly personal activity, REMAKE is a richly rewarding experience—emotionally, narratively and philosophically.” – Jonathan Romney, Screen International

screenings.title: Amadeus (70mm)
screenings.description: Producer Paul Zaentz in person on August 9 Dir. Milos Forman. 1984, 160 mins. U.S./France. 70mm. With F. Murray Abraham, Tom Hulce, Elizabeth Berridge, Jeffrey Jones, Christine Ebersole, Simon Callow, Cynthia Nixon. Milos Forman’s thrilling, Best Picture–winning adaptation of Peter Shaffer’s play may be, without parallel, the greatest cinematic evocation of artistic jealousy, centering on the mythic rivalry between Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and Antonio Salieri in 18th-century Vienna. Court composer for Emperor Joseph II, Salieri grows increasingly resentful of the ease with which the crass, childlike musician writes his works of astonishing beauty, leading to tragedy. Personifying the timeless, fruitless struggle between genius and mediocrity, Amadeus is a film of operatic force and keen wit, featuring brilliant performances by both Tom Hulce as Mozart and especially an Oscar-winning F. Murray Abraham as his envious competitor. Buy tickets for August 7 Buy tickets for August 9 Tickets: $25 / 25% discount for MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership.

screenings.title: Blood Brunch
screenings.description: Calling all Bloodeaters, Love Butchers and Neon Maniacs! The lights go down, the screen lights up and every one of your senses is flooded with ghastly terror from beyond the fetid grave. Spend your Sundays drenched in blood and quivering in fear with a mystery movie—as in, we don’t tell you what we’re showing until you see the title on the screen—that is at least 20 years old.

screenings.title: Mary Oliver: Saved by the Beauty of the World
screenings.description: If poetry had a pop icon, Mary Oliver would be it. Celebrated bestseller, Pulitzer Prize winner, lover of dogs and long walks in the woods, openly queer but intensely private, Oliver was America’s unlikely contemporary mystic, stalking the ponds and forests of Cape Cod for nearly 50 years in order to open herself – and her readers – to the known and unknowable world. From a lonely childhood to literary fame, Oliver’s life was shaped by devotion to nature, paying attention, and the long journey toward learning to love and to be loved. Her poems inspire liberals and conservatives, atheists and believers, naturalists and urbanites, speaking directly to contemporary anxieties about attention, presence, and the human relationship with the natural world – issues that feel especially pressing in an era of climate crisis, digital distraction, and social fragmentation.

screenings.title: Sherman's March
screenings.description: U.S., 1986 Written and directed by Ross McElwee Approx. 158 min. Armed with a 16mm camera and a grant to make a documentary about the lingering aftermath of William Tecumseh Sherman’s 1864 march to the sea, Ross McElwee gets sidetracked. After his girlfriend breaks up with him, Ross shifts his attention from the historical to the personal, to the battlefield of modern love, and embarks on a sociological chronicle that documents the courting rites and rituals of the New South. A generous and humanistic portrait of several remarkable women that Ross meets along the way, Sherman’s March sketches its characters with novelistic sensitivity: Pat, an aspiring actress with a yen for Burt Reynolds; Claudia, a roller-skating interior designer; Jackie, the activist whose anti-nuclear advocacy dovetails with Ross’s deepest fears; and above all, Charleen Swansea, Ross’s mentor and a one-woman Greek chorus of unsolicited romantic counsel. A landmark of first-person filmmaking that presaged everything from Michael Moore to reality TV. A Little Field Films Restoration with support from Cinema Conservancy, Harvard Film Archive, and The Library of Congress. Restoration Produced by Mark Meatto. Restoration Supervised by Ross McElwee. screenings.title: The Samurai and the Prisoner
screenings.description: When Lord Murashige Araki (Masahiro Motoki) rises up against the tyrannical Nobunaga Oda (Masaki Suda), he finds himself besieged within the walls of his own castle. Isolated, he is confronted with a series of mysterious crimes that shatter the fragile order of his court, plunging the fortress into fear and suspicion. With Oda’s army closing in and a traitor hiding among his ranks, Murashige is forced into an uneasy alliance with Kanbei Kuroda (Masaki Suda), a brilliant yet dangerous strategist held prisoner in the dungeon. Helped by his wife Chiyoho (Yuriko Yoshitaka) and his most loyal generals, Murashige must uncover the truth before the castle falls.

screenings.title: The Kid
screenings.description: Regarded as the Tramp’s first jump into feature films, this family-friendly six-reeler shows Chaplin at his most brilliant and most sentimental, plumbing memories of his own boyhood of almost Dickensian deprivation. The Tramp adopts an abandoned boy, played by soon-to-be-child-superstar Jackie Coogan, and fights against remarkable odds to keep the lad at his side. Gives us some of the most moving passages in Chaplin’s nakedly emotional filmography, including Charlie’s desperate search through city poorhouses for his missing charge, and the visualization of a poor boy’s imagining of heaven.

screenings.title: The Odyssey (35mm Screening)
screenings.description: Christopher Nolan’s next film, The Odyssey, is a mythic action epic shot across the world using brand new IMAX® film technology. The film brings Homer’s foundational saga to IMAX® film screens for the first time and opens in theaters everywhere on July 17, 2026.

screenings.title: Michael Mann's Manhunter: The Final Cut
screenings.description: Mann’s genre-defining serial-killer thriller returns in a stunning new restoration overseen by the filmmaker himself. A retired criminal profiler (William Petersen) reluctantly returns to the FBI to help track down a murderer and is forced to consult an expert—the imprisoned Dr. Hannibal Lecktor (Brian Cox in a subtly chilling performance). Adapted from the first of Thomas Harris’s Lecktor novels, MANHUNTER’s supporting cast includes Tom Noonan as the hunted killer, and three-time Oscar nominee Joan Allen.

screenings.title: Rebecca
screenings.description: “Last night I dreamt I went to Manderlay again…” Hitchcock was still a newly arrived UK import when this gothic thriller/romance, based on the novel of the same title by Daphne du Maurier, took Outstanding Production (later “Best Picture”) honors at the Academy Awards. Joan Fontaine stars as a terribly self-conscious young woman, never identified by name, who becomes enamored with a saturnine, aristocratic widower, Maxim de Winter (Laurence Olivier, fresh from Wuthering Heights)—and, once she’s been taken as his bride, obsessed with his late wife’s phantom presence in their home on the Cornwall coast. A marvel of directorial assurance that turns the screws with poise and panache.

screenings.title: Olmo
screenings.description: Olmo just wants to be a normal teenager and hang out with his best friend, but he must help care for his bedridden father. When Olmo gets invited to a party by his beautiful neighbor, he will do whatever he can to meet up with her while embarking on an adventure of mischief, laughs, and chaos. As the night unfolds, he may come to love the very place he’s spent so long trying to escape: his home. In English and Spanish with English subtitles.

screenings.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day
screenings.description: Four years have passed since the events of No Way Home, and Peter is now an adult living entirely alone, having voluntarily erased himself from the lives and memories of those he loves. Crime-fighting in a New York that no longer knows his name, he’s devoted himself entirely to protecting his city — a full-time Spider-Man — but as the demands on him intensify, the pressure sparks a surprising physical evolution that threatens his existence, even as a strange new pattern of crimes gives rise to one of the most powerful threats he has ever faced.

screenings.title: Favorites of the Moon
screenings.description: Having relocated to France in 1982, Iosseliani wasted no time in showing the world he hadn’t left his singular gifts behind upon leaving Georgia, taking home the Special Jury Prize at the 41st Venice International Film Festival for this puckish panoramic comedy about dizzying reversals of fortune and everyday acts of larceny, petty and otherwise. Terrorists, chanteuses, antique dealers, police inspectors, street walkers, and street sweepers all have a part to play in this farcical fable located at the intersection of Dickens and Tati, which follows the circulation of two precious objects—a Limoges porcelain dinner service and a portrait of a Belle Époque–era aristocratic beauty—as they’re passed from one pair of hands to another, and up and down the socioeconomic hierarchy, in Paris’s 13th arrondissement. Co-written with regular Polanski collaborator Gérard Brach, and featuring a very fresh-faced Mathieu Amalric in his very first film role.

screenings.title: Highway Hypnosis
screenings.description: Between the years of 1974 to 1979, not long after Manson Family trials had concluded, enigmatic artist and connoisseur of fringe culture, John Aes-Nihil, embarked on a project to “re-stage” the events leading up to the infamous Tate-LaBianca murders as a series of faux home movies, based on the legend that the Family had at one point stolen camera equipment to document their actions. The resulting feature— which, coincidentally, premiered in 1984 at EZTV alongside HIGHWAY HYPNOSIS— truly lives up to its filmmaker’s namesake Aesthetic Nihilism: Shot entirely on Super8mm and completely silent save for an accompanying soundtrack mostly comprised of music made by the Family itself (plus a little Patty Duke for good measure). The film re-frames the Manson Family story as a first-person travelogue across Southern California, imbued with chillingly realistic detail as we bear (false) witness to one of the most notorious events of the American century.

screenings.title: The Odyssey (DCP)
screenings.description: Odysseus, king of Ithaca, embarks on a perilous journey to return home after the Trojan War.

screenings.title: The Big Cheese
screenings.description: A scrappy team of eccentric American cheesemongers defies tradition to take on the world’s top cheese masters at the Mondial du Fromage, battling cultural clashes, personal struggles, and melting cheese in pursuit of respect, redemption, and a historic victory.

screenings.title: Jimmy
screenings.description: Shot in dreamy 16mm black and white, Yasshadai Owens’ debut feature Jimmy offers an intimate, speculative portrait of what a young James Baldwin may have experienced during his first trip to Paris in 1948. (credit: Toronto International Film Festival)

screenings.title: The Invite
screenings.description: Joe (Seth Rogen) and Angela’s (Olivia Wilde) marriage is on thin ice. When they invite their enigmatic upstairs neighbors (Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton) for a dinner party, the night spirals into unexpected places. Have they reignited the spark or lit the match that burns it all down? A remake of the 2020 Spanish film The People Upstairs, Olivia Wilde’s star-studded take on a dinner party dramedy (written by Will McCormack and Rashida Jones) is a timely portrait of a modern marriage, teeming with wit, belly laughs, and a surprising poignancy.

screenings.title: American Pachuco
screenings.description: Groundbreaking Chicano activist/director Luis Valdez mounted agitprop performances on flatbed trucks in the 1960s with his El Teatro Campesino, mobilizing California farmworkers to secure their first union contract; authored Zoot Suit, the first Chicano play on Broadway, and directed the 1981 screen adaptation, starring Edward James Olmos; and wrote and directed the highest-grossing Hollywood Latino movie in history, the Ritchie Valens biopic, LA BAMBA. AMERICAN PACHUCO (Valdez defines pachucos as Mexican-American “street cats with style”) playfully tracks his extraordinary life and career, with rarely seen footage from his subversive theater and television work, and interviews with Valdez; actors Olmos (who narrates the film in his ZOOT SUIT pachuco voice), Lou Diamond Phillips, and Cheech Marin; labor activist Dolores Huerta; and Linda Ronstadt. Presented with support from The Robert E. Appel Fund for Spanish and Portuguese Language Films, The Richard Brick, Geri Ashur, and Sara Bershtel Fund for Social Justice Documentaries, and The Roy Lichtenstein Foundation Fund 2026 93 MIN. USA IN ENGLISH AND SPANISH WITH ENGLISH SUBTITLES

As the night unfolds, he may come to love the very place he’s spent so long trying to escape: his home. In English and Spanish with English subtitles.

screenings.title: The Third Man
screenings.description: U.K./U.S., 1949 Directed by Carol Reed Screenplay by Graham Greene Starring Joseph Cotten, Alida Valli, Trevor Howard, and Orson Welles as Harry Lime Music by Anton Karas Cinematography by Robert Krasker WINNER Academy Award® – Best Cinematography, 1950 WINNER Cannes Film Festival – Palme d’Or, 1949 Approx. 104 min. 35mm. In rubble-strewn postwar Vienna, its occupation divided among four powers, Joseph Cotten’s pulp Western writer Holly Martins arrives to meet up with his old friend Harry Lime, only to find that he’s dead—or is he? And as the supremely naïve Cotten, a monoglot stranger in a strange land, descends through the levels of deception, and as he discovers his own friend’s corruption, the moral choices loom. A triumph of atmosphere—with its Vienna locations (including the gigantic Riesenrad ferris wheel and the dripping sewers), its tilted camera angles, its Robert Krasker-shot shadows, and Anton Karas’ unforgettable zither theme—and with its stars in perhaps their most iconic roles: bereted Trevor Howard at his most Britishly military; Alida Valli, here truly enigmatic and Garboesque; and Welles’ Harry Lime, arriving in one of the greatest star entrances ever, and adding the famous “cuckoo clock” speech to Greene’s original script, with the whole topped by its legendary, almost endlessly drawn-out finale shot. Winner of the Palme d’Or at the Cannes Film Festival and an Academy Award® for Best Cinematography, along with many other awards and nominations, THE THIRD MAN has appeared repeatedly on “Best of All-Time” lists of the past 75 years. Presented with support from The Robert Jolin Osborne Endowed Fund for American Classic Cinema of the 1930s, ’40s, and ’50s and The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film A RIALTO PICTURES RELEASE

screenings.title: The Fence
screenings.description: A vast public works project in West Africa. Horn (Matt Dillon), the construction site manager, and Cal (Tom Blyth), a young engineer, share lodging behind the double gates of their compound. Leone (Mia McKenna-Bruce), Horn’s recent bride, comes to join them the same night that a man (Isaach De Bankole) appears at the fence. His name is Alboury. Like a specter in the darkness, he demands the body of his brother who died earlier that day on the site. He will hound the two men all night long until they return it, as Leone watches the disaster play out before her.

screenings.title: Conversation Piece
screenings.description: Burt Lancaster reunited with his The Leopard director for Visconti’s penultimate film, an elegant odd-couple chamber drama in which the leonine “Boit” plays a graying American intellectual immured from the modern world in his Roman palazzo—until, that is, his fortress of solitude is invaded by a pushy Marquise (Silvana Mangano) who browbears him into renting her his unused top floor to be used as a gilded cage for her boytoy, Konrad (Helmut Berger), a ’68 activist turned gigolo to the gentry, who interrupts the old man’s bedtime Mozart with Italopop and nude pot parties. Best known for his work in the epic vein, Visconti here renders verbal close-combat every bit as thrilling as any dispatch from the battlefields of Europe.

screenings.title: And Then There Was Light
screenings.description: The confrontation of a traditional rural/agrarian culture bound to the land and the cycles of the seasons and an urban/industrial society that has largely forgotten these ties, an abiding concern of Iosseliani’s cinema, plays out against a backdrop entirely new to his work in this fable-like homage to silent cinema, intertitles and all. In the village of Casamance in southern Senegal, home to the Jola people, life goes on much as it has since time immemorial, with its gossip-mongering, its local scandals, its rituals of field labor and midday meals—until, that is, new European machinery begins to arrive on the scene, its intended use: deforestation of the region and exploitation of its natural resources. “There is an interweaving, an interdependence, of real life and ancient poetry… The film’s texture is not raw, not naturalistic. In Africa, as in his native Georgia, [Iosseliani] enters into a kind of symbiosis with the ‘spirit’ of the country.” —Le Monde

screenings.title: A Child of My Own
screenings.description: This new hybrid documentary from the Oscar-nominated director of The Mole Agent and The Eternal Memory follows the shocking tale of a woman desperate for a baby. Burdened by family and societal expectations, she fakes a pregnancy and gets tangled up in a crime.

screenings.title: The Chaser
screenings.description: Drawing inspiration from the gristly exploits of South Korean serial killer Yoo Young-chul, Na’s astonishingly assured directorial debut stars Ha Jung-woo as a sadistic killer, Ji Yeong-min, and Kim Yoon-seok as Joong-ho, an ex-detective with a checkered past now running a prostitution ring. After helplessly watching his stable of employees disappear and dwindle, Joong-ho sets out to find the sicko responsible—and in the course of a sleepless night of cat and mouse, finds he has to contend not only with the killer’s calculating intelligence and red herring misleads, but with an incompetent police force and a thicket of bureaucratic barriers that seem to have been erected with the specific purpose of allowing the guilty to get away clean. Winner of Best Actor, Best Film, and Best Director at Korea’s Grand Bell Awards, The Chaser is both a precision-tuned white-knuckle thriller and an agonized exploration of insoluble moral conundrums.

screenings.description: A vast public works project in West Africa. Horn (Matt Dillon), the construction site manager, and Cal (Tom Blyth), a young engineer, share lodging behind the double gates of their compound. Leone (Mia McKenna-Bruce), Horn’s recent bride, comes to join them the same night that a man (Isaach De Bankole) appears at the fence. His name is Alboury. Like a specter in the darkness, he demands the body of his brother who died earlier that day on the site. He will hound the two men all night long until they return it, as Leone watches the disaster play out before her.

In the company of his new friends, including the mysterious and mercurial Gloria (Lee of PAST LIVES), Ed has the uncanny feeling of merging with his younger self. screenings.title: Center Stage
screenings.description: Hong Kong, 1991 Directed by Stanley Kwan Starring Maggie Cheung, Han Chin, Carina Lau, Tony Leung Ka-fai In Cantonese, Mandarin, and English Approx. 155 min. International superstar Maggie Cheung (IN THE MOOD FOR LOVE) embodies tragic screen siren Ruan Lingyu, known as the “Greta Garbo of China,” in this unconventional biopic by Hong Kong New Wave master Stanley Kwan (ROUGE). Praised for her moving and emotive onscreen presence, Ruan’s private life, which was frequent fodder for the vicious Shanghai tabloids, began to mirror the melodramas which brought her fame, culminating in her suicide at age 24. Kwan and Cheung paint a kaleidoscopic yet intimate portrait of the ill-fated actress, deftly blending lush period drama, archival footage, and metatextual documentary sequences of Cheung reflecting on Ruan’s legacy. The result is, much like the films of Ruan Lingyu themselves, “tender, vivid, and almost overwhelmingly moving” (Time Out). Presented by Fortune Star Media Limited, the restoration of the film was carried out from the original 35mm picture and optical soundtrack negative. The prints were repaired, cleaned and scanned in Hong Kong, then digitally restored in 4K resolution in Bologna, Italy by L'Immagine Ritrovata. Endorsed by the director, Stanley Kwan, the color correction was completed by Interface Video Production Ltd in Hong Kong. Presented with support from The Reginald S. Reinhardt, Ling-Makekau Fund for Asia-Pacific Films A FILM MOVEMENT RELEASE

screenings.title: Mary Oliver: Saved by the Beauty of the World
screenings.description: If poetry had a pop icon, Mary Oliver would be it. Celebrated bestseller, Pulitzer Prize winner, lover of dogs and long walks in the woods, openly queer but intensely private, Oliver was America’s unlikely contemporary mystic, stalking the ponds and forests of Cape Cod for nearly 50 years in order to open herself – and her readers – to the known and unknowable world. From a lonely childhood to literary fame, Oliver’s life was shaped by devotion to nature, paying attention, and the long journey toward learning to love and to be loved. Her poems inspire liberals and conservatives, atheists and believers, naturalists and urbanites, speaking directly to contemporary anxieties about attention, presence, and the human relationship with the natural world – issues that feel especially pressing in an era of climate crisis, digital distraction, and social fragmentation.

screenings.title: Bouchra
screenings.description: Multihyphenate artists Barki and Bennani’s playful animation/live-action hybrid film à clef offers up a delightfully idiosyncratic look at the travails of the queer expat artist. The title character here is imagined as an anthropomorphic jackal inhabiting a New York City filled with other like critters, a young filmmaker simultaneously dealing with creative crises, her rocky relationship with her mother back in Casablanca, and the pleasures and perils of sex in the city. Drawing on real phone calls and myriad other correspondences, with voice talent courtesy of the directing duo’s friends and family members, this lay-it-on-the-line autofiction is at once startlingly light on its feet and densely layered with insight, not least into the feelings that come of shakily straddling two cultures while belonging fully to neither.

screenings.title: Toute une nuit
screenings.description: Emotions boil over and thunder rolls during one oppressively humid summer night in Brussels in Akerman’s tender and melancholy film of brief encounters, furtive embraces, nocturnal despair, yearning vigils, and pregnant silences. A string of self-contained vignettes, precisely composed and parsimonious in use of dialogue, their abiding air of tension occasionally rent by cloudbursts of frenzied feeling, Toute une nuit may be regarded, like the filmmaker’s News from Home, as an inimitable twist on the “city symphony” genre, laying its scenes in the bars, cafes, and streets of Akerman’s hometown. “A comédie sentimentale treated as a choreographed dance.” —Cahiers du Cinéma

screenings.title: Sherman's March
screenings.description: U.S., 1986 Written and directed by Ross McElwee Approx. 158 min. Armed with a 16mm camera and a grant to make a documentary about the lingering aftermath of William Tecumseh Sherman’s 1864 march to the sea, Ross McElwee gets sidetracked. After his girlfriend breaks up with him, Ross shifts his attention from the historical to the personal, to the battlefield of modern love, and embarks on a sociological chronicle that documents the courting rites and rituals of the New South. A generous and humanistic portrait of several remarkable women that Ross meets along the way, Sherman’s March sketches its characters with novelistic sensitivity: Pat, an aspiring actress with a yen for Burt Reynolds; Claudia, a roller-skating interior designer; Jackie, the activist whose anti-nuclear advocacy dovetails with Ross’s deepest fears; and above all, Charleen Swansea, Ross’s mentor and a one-woman Greek chorus of unsolicited romantic counsel. A landmark of first-person filmmaking that presaged everything from Michael Moore to reality TV. screenings.title: White Nights

screenings.title: La Collectionneuse
screenings.description: The third entry in Rohmer’s Six Moral Tales series, in which cinematographer Néstor Almendros takes magnificent advantage of the glorious natural light of the French Riviera, is a deceptively lovely film about less-than-lovely behavior, an ironic study of male acquisitiveness and priggish high-handedness in which two friends, a fastidious painter, Daniel (Pommereulle), and a dilettante art dealer, Adrien (Patrick Bauchau), find themselves sharing a summer house near Saint-Tropez with a third occupant, a young woman named Haydée Politoff, who winds up in the middle of their psychological gamesmanship. Written in collaboration with its three leads, this gold-hued depiction of moral rot may be the film in which Rohmer’s mature style first appears fully formed.

screenings.title: Millionaires' Express
screenings.description: Arguably the most formidable ensemble cast in the history of Hong Kong cinema assembled on the set of Hung’s Eastern Western, in which reformed outlaw Sammo teams with Sheriff (played by Yuen Biao) to protect their impoverished rural hometown from a sudden influx of desperate characters, all plotting to make a fast fortune off the passengers of a brand new luxury train scheduled to pass through on the Shanghai-Chengdu line. Veteran stalwarts like Jimmy Wang Yu and James Tien rub shoulders with fresh talents like Rosamund Kwan and Cynthia Rothrock, Japanese ninjas vie with Soviet bandits, and the spectacular action and inspired slapstick scarcely lets up for a minute in this deliriously entertaining action-adventure vaudeville.

screenings.description: Hong Kong, 1991 Directed by Stanley Kwan Starring Maggie Cheung, Han Chin, Carina Lau, Tony Leung Ka-fai In Cantonese, Mandarin, and English Approx. 155 min. International superstar Maggie Cheung (IN THE MOOD FOR LOVE) embodies tragic screen siren Ruan Lingyu, known as the “Greta Garbo of China,” in this unconventional biopic by Hong Kong New Wave master Stanley Kwan (ROUGE). Praised for her moving and emotive onscreen presence, Ruan’s private life, which was frequent fodder for the vicious Shanghai tabloids, began to mirror the melodramas which brought her fame, culminating in her suicide at age 24. Kwan and Cheung paint a kaleidoscopic yet intimate portrait of the ill-fated actress, deftly blending lush period drama, archival footage, and metatextual documentary sequences of Cheung reflecting on Ruan’s legacy. The result is, much like the films of Ruan Lingyu themselves, “tender, vivid, and almost overwhelmingly moving” (Time Out). Presented by Fortune Star Media Limited, the restoration of the film was carried out from the original 35mm picture and optical soundtrack negative. The prints were repaired, cleaned and scanned in Hong Kong, then digitally restored in 4K resolution in Bologna, Italy by L'Immagine Ritrovata. Endorsed by the director, Stanley Kwan, the color correction was completed by Interface Video Production Ltd in Hong Kong. Presented with support from The Reginald S. Reinhardt, Ling-Makekau Fund for Asia-Pacific Films A FILM MOVEMENT RELEASE

screenings.description: Alongside his more touted multi-character panoramas, Altman also had a fondness for small-scale dramas investigating the complexities of female psychology, and of these none is greater than the ineffable 3 Women, which finds Shelley Duvall, Sissy Spacek, and Janice Rule thrown together at a health spa in the California desert that caters to the elderly. screenings.title: Stalking Chernobyl
screenings.description: After showcasing two of her documentaries last year, Spectacle is proud to host the New York City premiere of iara lee’s latest feature, THE SAMI SONG OF SURVIVAL. Throughout her prolific career as a cultural film essayist, iara lee intentionally sought out Indigenous voices in political peril. Inspired by her 2010 documentary and participation in the Gaza Freedom Flotilla, iara lee established the Cultures of Resistance Network to raise awareness of folks on the margins and the art they create. With lee’s latest, THE SAMI SONG OF SURVIVAL, we’re witnesses to the Sami people, an Indigenous group based in Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Russia. Undergoing constant oppression against imperial forces and racist colonialism, with one Sami man in particular hypothesizing, “Art could be a weapon”. A motivating mantra that sums up the essence of iara lee’s filmmaking ethos, Spectacle Theater will be screening this alongside two power-defying docs: K2 & THE INVISIBLE FOOTMEN and STALKING CHERNOBYL.

screenings.title: Dread Beat an Blood
screenings.description: About DREAD BEAT AN BLOOD: “[A] gem... a portrait of the artist as principled activist.” – Sasha Frere-Jones, 4Columns “Fantastic... An amazing snapshot of the time of the pre-Brixton riots... This is so relevant a movie. That’s what makes it so good.” – Gilles Peterson, BBC “A fascinating document of LKJ in his time and place, touring with the sound systems, strolling through the market and visiting Tulse Hill schools, vividly capturing black British culture in a country on the cusp of Thatcherism, just a few months before the Brixton uprising.” – Stephen Troussé, Uncut “An invaluable document of Brixton, an area that was already at the front lines of the anti-racist struggle, the streets in which people would soon rise up in rebellion. That sense of latent frustration simmers in every frame. It is Johnson himself who articulates that frustration, honing that anger into art via his poetry.” – Kevin Mccaighy, The Quietus About Linton Kwesi Johnson: “If any young artists need to know about longevity and integrity, Linton Kwesi Johnson is the one to look to... He knew his path and he walked it. His words are still relevant and that reggae bass is still vibrating.” – Steve McQueen “Linton Kwesi Johnson’s impact on the cultural landscape over the last half-century has been colossal and multi-generational.” – The Guardian “He’s written the anthems for a generation who felt oppressed and victimized... He’s now celebrated as one of this country’s most influential cultural commentators.” – BBC “A revolutionary poet for our times.” – Jacobin “The Poet Laureate of Black Britain.” – Paul Gilroy “The roots of hip-hop run deep, and among the deepest branches remains Linton Kwesi Johnson, the Jamaican-born, British-raised poet, writer, and performer often hailed as the father of dub poetry.” – David Browne, Rolling Stone

screenings.description: 30 years after vanishing at sea, the eponymous fishing vessel mysteriously reappears in the harbor of a seaside village. The astonished local citizens see its return as a sign, convinced the luck of their economically devastated community may turn, if only the ship sails again. Joining the crew are Nick (George MacKay), desperate to provide for his young family, and Liam (Callum Turner), a mysterious drifter eager to escape his past. When they return from their voyage, nothing is as they remember it. Shooting in supersaturated color on a 16mm Bolex and constructing all the sound in post, Mark Jenkin’s hallucinatory time-travel mystery further solidifies him as one of the most singular artists working in film today.

screenings.description: Los Angeles cabbie Max Durocher (Jamie Foxx) is in for the toughest fare of his working life when he picks up one Vincent (Tom Cruise, natty in charcoal gray sharkskin suit), a jazz enthusiast and professional hitman who quite firmly insists that his driver accompany him on his evening’s rounds, leaving a trail of bodies in his wake. screenings.title: Remake

screenings.title: Mary Oliver: Saved by the Beauty of the World
screenings.description: If poetry had a pop icon, Mary Oliver would be it. Celebrated bestseller, Pulitzer Prize winner, lover of dogs and long walks in the woods, openly queer but intensely private, Oliver was America’s unlikely contemporary mystic, stalking the ponds and forests of Cape Cod for nearly 50 years in order to open herself – and her readers – to the known and unknowable world. From a lonely childhood to literary fame, Oliver’s life was shaped by devotion to nature, paying attention, and the long journey toward learning to love and to be loved. Her poems inspire liberals and conservatives, atheists and believers, naturalists and urbanites, speaking directly to contemporary anxieties about attention, presence, and the human relationship with the natural world – issues that feel especially pressing in an era of climate crisis, digital distraction, and social fragmentation.

screenings.title: Vertigo
screenings.description: Dress up becomes a matter of fevered fixation in Hitchcock’s utterly intoxicating thriller, in which ex-cop-cum-snoop-for-hire Scottie Ferguson (Jimmy Stewart) sets out on a routine job tailing the mysterious Madeline (Kim Novak), an old pal’s wife—and soon finds himself in the center of a whirlpool of romantic obsession and supernatural quandaries, speeding towards a tragic denouement. Perennially on the short list of the greatest films of all time, Hitchcock’s film of death, desire, and doppelgangers—a key inspiration haunting every frame of Chantal Akerman's La Captive—has lost none of its ability to simultaneously seduce and repel. “One of the landmarks—not merely of the movies, but of 20th-century art.”—Dave Kehr, Chicago Reader

screenings.title: The Green Room
screenings.description: One of Truffaut’s most personal and beautiful films, photographed “in fecund greens and withering yellows” [Dave Kehr, Chicago Reader] by DP Néstor Almendros, and one of the least known of Truffaut’s major works—audiences, it seems, weren’t ready for this stark rumination on death from a filmmaker known for his gentle humor and twinkling personability. Truffaut, not far removed from his own premature end, stars himself alongside Nathalie Baye in this adaptation of Henry James’s short story “Altar of the Dead,” about a newspaper obituary writer who has become obsessed with the memory of friends departed from this mortal coil, represented here by images of the director’s own deceased loved ones.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day
screenings.description: Four years have passed since the events of No Way Home, and Peter is now an adult living entirely alone, having voluntarily erased himself from the lives and memories of those he loves. screenings.title: The Fence
screenings.description: A vast public works project in West Africa. Horn (Matt Dillon), the construction site manager, and Cal (Tom Blyth), a young engineer, share lodging behind the double gates of their compound. Leone (Mia McKenna-Bruce), Horn’s recent bride, comes to join them the same night that a man (Isaach De Bankole) appears at the fence. His name is Alboury. Like a specter in the darkness, he demands the body of his brother who died earlier that day on the site. He will hound the two men all night long until they return it, as Leone watches the disaster play out before her.

screenings.title: Sherman's March
screenings.description: U.S., 1986 Written and directed by Ross McElwee Approx. 158 min. Armed with a 16mm camera and a grant to make a documentary about the lingering aftermath of William Tecumseh Sherman’s 1864 march to the sea, Ross McElwee gets sidetracked. After his girlfriend breaks up with him, Ross shifts his attention from the historical to the personal, to the battlefield of modern love, and embarks on a sociological chronicle that documents the courting rites and rituals of the New South. A generous and humanistic portrait of several remarkable women that Ross meets along the way, Sherman’s March sketches its characters with novelistic sensitivity: Pat, an aspiring actress with a yen for Burt Reynolds; Claudia, a roller-skating interior designer; Jackie, the activist whose anti-nuclear advocacy dovetails with Ross’s deepest fears; and above all, Charleen Swansea, Ross’s mentor and a one-woman Greek chorus of unsolicited romantic counsel. A landmark of first-person filmmaking that presaged everything from Michael Moore to reality TV. A Little Field Films Restoration with support from Cinema Conservancy, Harvard Film Archive, and The Library of Congress. Restoration Produced by Mark Meatto. Restoration Supervised by Ross McElwee.
